title: Chapter 130 — The Hat
paragraphs: And now that, at the proper time and place, after so long and wide a preliminary cruise, Ahab — all other whaling waters swept — seemed to have chased his foe into a fold of the ocean, to slay him there the more securely; now that he found himself close to the very latitude and longitude where his tormenting wound had been inflicted; now that a vessel had been hailed which, only the day before, had actually encountered Moby Dick; and now that all his successive meetings with various ships had, in their contrasting ways, combined to show the demonic indifference with which the white whale tore his hunters, whether sinning or sinned against — now there lurked something in the old man's eyes that feeble souls could hardly bear to see. Like the never-setting polar star, which through the long, six-month arctic night keeps up its piercing, steady, central gaze, Ahab's purpose now gleamed fixedly down upon the constant midnight of the gloomy crew. It so dominated them that all their forebodings, doubts, misgivings and fears were forced to hide beneath their souls, and not sprout a single blade or leaf.

In this foreshadowing interval, too, all humor, forced or natural, vanished. Stubb no longer tried to raise a smile; Starbuck no longer tried to check one. Joy and sorrow, hope and fear alike seemed ground to the finest dust, and powdered for the time in the clamped mortar of Ahab's iron soul. Like machines, they moved dumbly about the deck, always aware that the old man's despot eye was on them.

But had you studied him closely in his more secret, private hours, when he thought no eye but one was on him, you would have seen that just as Ahab's eyes awed the crew's, the inscrutable Parsee's glance awed his — or at least, somehow, in some wild way, affected it at times. Such an added, gliding strangeness now began to surround the thin Fedallah, and such ceaseless shudderings shook him, that the men eyed him doubtfully, half uncertain, it seemed, whether he really was a mortal substance or else a tremulous shadow cast upon the deck by some unseen being's body. And that shadow was always hovering there. For not even by night had Fedallah ever been known for certain to sleep or go below. He would stand still for hours, but he never sat or leaned; his wan but wondrous eyes said plainly — We two watchmen never rest.

Nor could the sailors now step onto the deck at any time, night or day, without finding Ahab there before them — either standing in his pivot-hole, or pacing the planks exactly between two unvarying limits, the main-mast and the mizen; or else they saw him standing in the cabin-scuttle, his living foot advanced upon the deck as if to take a step, his hat slouched heavily over his eyes. So however motionless he stood, and however many days and nights were added on in which he had not swung in his hammock, still, hidden beneath that slouching hat, they could never tell for certain whether, for all this, his eyes were actually closed at times, or whether he was still intently watching them — no matter that he stood like that in the scuttle for a whole hour at a stretch, and the unheeded night-damp gathered in beads of dew on that stone-carved coat and hat. The clothes the night had wet, the next day's sunshine dried on him; and so, day after day and night after night, he no longer went below the planks; whatever he wanted from the cabin, he sent for.

He ate in the same open air — that is, his only two meals, breakfast and dinner; supper he never touched. Nor did he reap his beard, which grew darkly, all gnarled, like the unearthed roots of blown-over trees, which still grow idly on at the naked base though they have perished in the green growth above. But though his whole life had now become one watch on deck, and though the Parsee's mystic watch was as unbroken as his own, these two never seemed to speak — one man to the other — except when, at long intervals, some passing, unimportant matter made it necessary. Though such a potent spell seemed secretly to join the two, openly, and to the awe-struck crew, they seemed as far apart as the poles. If by day they happened to speak one word, by night both were dumb men, as far as the slightest exchange of words went. At times, for the longest hours, without a single hail, they stood far apart in the starlight, Ahab in his scuttle, the Parsee by the mainmast, but still gazing fixedly at each other — as if in the Parsee Ahab saw his forethrown shadow, and in Ahab the Parsee saw his abandoned substance.

And yet, somehow, Ahab — in his own proper self, as he was daily, hourly and every instant commandingly revealed to his subordinates — Ahab seemed an independent lord, and the Parsee only his slave. Then again, both seemed yoked together, with an unseen tyrant driving them: the lean shadow alongside the solid rib. For whatever this Parsee might be, all rib and keel was solid Ahab.

At the first faintest glimmering of dawn, his iron voice was heard from aft — "Man the mast-heads!" — and all through the day, until after sunset and after twilight, the same voice was heard every hour, at the striking of the helmsman's bell — "What do you see? — sharp! sharp!"

But when three or four days had slipped by since meeting the children-seeking Rachel, and still no spout had been seen, the monomaniac old man seemed to distrust his crew's loyalty — at least, that of nearly all of them except the Pagan harpooners. He even seemed to suspect that Stubb and Flask might willingly overlook the sight he was seeking. But if these suspicions really were his, he shrewdly refrained from putting them into words, however much his actions might seem to hint at them.

"I will have the first sight of the whale myself," he said. "Aye! Ahab must have the doubloon!" And with his own hands he rigged a nest of basketed bowlines; and sending a man aloft with a single-sheaved block to fasten to the main-mast head, he took the two ends of the rope rove down through it; and attaching one to his basket, he prepared a belaying pin for the other end, so as to fasten it at the rail. This done, with that end still in his hand and standing beside the pin, he looked round at his crew, sweeping from one to another, letting his glance rest long on Daggoo, Queequeg and Tashtego, but avoiding Fedallah; and then, settling his firm, trusting eye on the chief mate, he said — "Take the rope, sir — I give it into your hands, Starbuck." Then, settling himself in the basket, he gave the word for them to hoist him to his perch, Starbuck being the one who finally made the rope fast, and who afterwards stood near it. And so, with one hand clinging round the royal mast, Ahab gazed out over the sea for miles and miles — ahead, astern, this side and that — within the wide, expanded circle commanded from so great a height.

When a sailor at sea, working with his hands at some high, almost isolated spot in the rigging that happens to offer no foothold, is hoisted up to that spot and held there by the rope, the rope's fastened end on deck is always given in strict charge to one particular man, who has the special watch of it. This is because, in such a wilderness of running rigging, whose various relations aloft cannot always be told with certainty from what can be seen of them on deck, and when the deck-ends of these ropes are being cast off from their fastenings every few minutes, it would be only a natural fatality if, without a constant watchman, the hoisted sailor were cast adrift through some carelessness of the crew and fell swooping down into the sea. So Ahab's proceedings in this matter were not unusual. The only strange thing about them seemed to be that Starbuck — almost the only man who had ever ventured to oppose him with anything even slightly approaching decisiveness, and one of those, too, whose faithfulness on the lookout he had seemed somewhat to doubt — it was strange that this was the very man he should choose as his watchman, freely placing his whole life in the hands of a man he otherwise distrusted.

Now, the first time Ahab was perched aloft, before he had been there ten minutes, one of those savage red-billed sea-hawks that so often fly annoyingly close around the manned mast-heads of whalemen in these latitudes — one of these birds came wheeling and screaming round his head in a maze of untrackably swift circlings. Then it shot a thousand feet straight up into the air, then spiraled downward, and went eddying round his head again.

But with his gaze fixed on the dim and distant horizon, Ahab seemed not to notice this wild bird; nor, indeed, would anyone else have noticed it much, since it was no uncommon occurrence; only now, almost the least heedful eye seemed to see some sort of cunning meaning in almost every sight.

"Your hat, your hat, sir!" the Sicilian seaman suddenly cried. He was posted at the mizzen-masthead and stood directly behind Ahab, though somewhat below his level, with a deep gulf of air between them.
But the dark wing was already before the old man's eyes, the long hooked beak at his head; and with a scream the black hawk shot away with his prize.

An eagle flew three times around Tarquin's head, lifting off his cap and then putting it back, and at that Tanaquil, his wife, declared that Tarquin would be king of Rome. But it was only because the cap was put back that the omen was counted good. Ahab's hat was never restored; the wild hawk flew on and on with it, far ahead of the prow, and at last disappeared; while from the point where it disappeared, a tiny black spot was dimly seen falling from that vast height into the sea.
